questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a reported p-value correctly
questions.stem: A researcher reports p = .03 for a diet intervention. What does this p-value indicate about the null hypothesis?

options.text: If the null were true, data this extreme would occur about 3% of the time
There is a 3 percent chance the treatment effect is zero in reality
options.misconception: treats p as posterior probability of no effect

options.text: The probability that the null hypothesis is true is only 3 percent
options.misconception: confuses p-value with probability the null is true

options.text: The effect size is 0.03, which is small but significant

questions.explanation: A p-value is the probability of data at least this extreme assuming the null hypothesis; it is not the probability the null is true or the effect size. The tempting reading treats p as a posterior probability.
questions.hint: Think conditional on the null being true.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Identify factors that widen a confidence interval
questions.stem: Which change would most widen a 95% confidence interval for a mean?

options.text: Increasing the sample size from 50 to 200
options.misconception: reverses the sample size effect on width

options.text: A larger standard deviation in the sample
Lowering the confidence level from 95% to 90%
Using a two-sided instead of one-sided interval

questions.explanation: Interval width grows with variability and shrinks with sample size; a larger standard deviation widens it. Bigger samples or lower levels narrow rather than widen the interval.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a p-value alone is insufficient
questions.stem: Why should a significant p-value be reported alongside an effect size?

answer.exemplar: A p-value only signals that an effect is unlikely under the null; an effect size reveals how large the effect is, which matters for practical importance and for comparing studies.

questions.explanation: Statistical significance does not imply magnitude or practical importance. Reporting effect size adds the missing information about how large and useful the effect is.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish statistical from practical significance

stimulus.body: A trial of a new study-skills app shows a mean gain of 0.4 points on a 100-point exam with p = .001. The gain is statistically significant but very small.

questions.stem: Given the app result, which conclusion is most appropriate?

options.text: The app is highly effective because p is very small
options.misconception: equates small p with large practical benefit

options.text: The result is meaningless because the gain is tiny
options.misconception: dismisses a real but small effect entirely

options.text: The p-value proves the app causes higher scores
The effect is real but likely too small to matter in practice

questions.explanation: A tiny p-value with a tiny gain shows a real but practically trivial effect. Practical significance requires judging magnitude against real-world value, not just p.
questions.hint: Judge the size, not just p.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: State what a correlation does and does not establish
questions.stem: Two variables have r = .70. What can be concluded?

options.text: The variables are linearly associated, not necessarily causal
One variable causes the other to change
The relationship is definitely nonlinear
70% of the variance in one is explained by the other

questions.explanation: A correlation measures linear association. It does not establish causation, linearity beyond the fitted line, or the proportion of variance explained (that is r-squared).

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Recognize a lurking variable in an association

stimulus.body: Ice cream sales and drowning incidents rise together each summer. A blogger claims ice cream causes drowning.

questions.stem: What best explains the observed association?

options.text: Ice cream consumption directly increases drowning risk
Drowning causes people to buy ice cream
The sample size is too small to trust the pattern
Hot weather increases both ice cream sales and swimming

questions.explanation: A lurking variable, hot weather, drives both outcomes. The association disappears or weakens once temperature is accounted for, so no causal claim is warranted.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Judge whether an observational design supports causation
questions.stem: A cohort study finds coffee drinkers have lower heart disease. Can we conclude coffee prevents heart disease?

options.text: No, observational data cannot rule out confounding
Yes, because the sample is large and representative
Yes, if the p-value is below .05
No, because correlation can never be positive

questions.explanation: Observational designs lack random assignment, so confounders may explain the link. A causal claim requires design features or assumptions that address confounding.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why non-equivalent groups threaten inference
questions.stem: A program group has pretest mean 72 and a control group 68. If the program adds 5 points, what is the posttest mean for the program group?
questions.explanation: Add the 5-point gain to the pretest mean of 72 to get 77. The groups started unequal, so the raw posttest gap overstates the program effect.

options.text: A guarantee that participation will improve health
A waiver of all legal rights by the participant
The researcher's personal contact details only
A statement that participation is voluntary and may be withdrawn

questions.explanation: Informed consent must state that participation is voluntary and can be withdrawn without penalty. It cannot promise benefits or demand rights waivers.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Recognize when ethics review is required

options.text: Yes, human subjects research generally requires review
No, because participants are peers
No, because the topic is low risk and familiar
Yes, but only if the study is published

questions.explanation: Research with human subjects generally requires ethics review regardless of perceived risk, peer status, or publication plans. Review protects participants.

options.text: The groups definitely differ in the population
The effect size must be large given the small p
The null is proven true because p is close to .05
The result is just below .05 and could be fragile

questions.explanation: A p-value just under .05 indicates a borderline result that may not replicate. It does not prove a population difference or imply a large effect.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Compute how sample size affects interval width
questions.stem: A 95% CI half-width is 4 with n=25. Assuming the same standard deviation, what is the half-width with n=100?
questions.explanation: Quadrupling sample size halves the standard error, so the half-width falls from 4 to 2. Width scales with one over the square root of n.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Calculate a simple effect size
questions.stem: Group A mean is 80 and group B mean is 74 with pooled SD 12. What is Cohen's d?
questions.explanation: Subtract 74 from 80 to get 6, then divide by 12 to obtain 0.5. This medium effect size complements the significance test.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate practical significance from a graph

stimulus.body: A bar chart compares two teaching methods. Method X scores 78.2 and Method Y 77.9 on a 100-point test, with a significant p-value.

questions.stem: What conclusion about practical significance is best?

options.text: The difference is real but negligible in practice
Method X is clearly superior for all classrooms
The p-value shows no effect exists
Method Y should be banned for poor results

questions.explanation: A 0.3-point gap with a significant p-value is real but negligible in practice. Practical significance requires judging whether the size matters to stakeholders.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Interpret r-squared from a scatterplot
questions.stem: A scatterplot shows r = .60 between study hours and exam score. What percent of variance is explained?
questions.explanation: Square .60 to get .36, then convert to 36 percent. r-squared gives the proportion of variance explained, not r itself.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Predict how controlling a third variable changes an association
questions.stem: Stage 1: Coffee drinking correlates with lower mortality. Stage 2: After controlling for age, the correlation weakens. What does this imply?

options.text: Age fully explains the original link
Controlling always strengthens correlations
Age partly confounded the original association
The sample must be biased

questions.explanation: A weakening association after control suggests age partly confounded the link. It does not prove full explanation, and control can either strengthen or weaken correlations.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Choose a design that supports causation
questions.stem: Which design best supports a causal claim about a new tutoring program?

options.text: A single-group pretest-posttest study
A case study of one successful student
A cross-sectional survey of users
A randomized controlled trial

questions.explanation: Random assignment balances confounders and supports causal inference. Single-group, cross-sectional, and case-study designs lack that protection.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Recognize a selection threat
questions.stem: Two classes differ in prior achievement before a new curriculum. What threat is present?

options.text: Selection, because groups differ at baseline
History, because events affect both classes
Attrition, because students drop out
Testing, because a pretest was given

questions.explanation: Baseline differences between groups indicate a selection threat. History, attrition, and testing are separate threats with different causes.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Judge whether consent is truly informed
questions.stem: A consent form is written at a college reading level for adult participants with limited literacy. Is consent adequate?

options.text: Yes, because adults can ask questions
Yes, if the form is legally reviewed
No, comprehension must match participant level
No, because consent is never needed for adults

questions.explanation: Informed consent requires comprehension at the participant's level. Legal review or the chance to ask questions does not fix unreadable language.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Identify a risk that increases review scrutiny
questions.stem: Which study feature most likely requires full board ethics review?

options.text: Anonymous survey of adult opinions
Secondary analysis of public data
Observation of public behavior only
Deception with delayed debriefing

questions.explanation: Deception with delayed debriefing poses more than minimal risk and typically needs full board review. Anonymous surveys and public data usually qualify for expedited or exempt review.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why p-values are not effect sizes
questions.stem: Why is a small p-value not evidence of a large effect?

answer.exemplar: A p-value measures compatibility of data with the null hypothesis, not magnitude; with a huge sample even a tiny difference can yield a very small p-value.

questions.explanation: Significance depends on sample size and variance as well as effect size. A small p can accompany a trivial effect when precision is high.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Identify the effect of confidence level on width
questions.stem: How does raising the confidence level from 90% to 99% affect interval width?

options.text: It widens the interval to capture more plausible values
It narrows the interval by reducing alpha
It has no effect if sample size is large
It changes the point estimate only

questions.explanation: Higher confidence requires a wider interval to cover the true parameter more often. Sample size affects width but does not remove the level effect.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Compare two studies using effect sizes
questions.stem: Study 1: p = .01, d = 0.2. Study 2: p = .06, d = 0.8. Which has the more important effect?

options.text: Study 1, because it is significant
They are equal because p-values differ slightly
Study 2, because its effect is larger
Neither, because p > .05 in Study 2

questions.explanation: Effect size indicates practical importance; Study 2's larger d matters more despite nonsignificance. Significance alone can mislead when samples differ.
questions.hint: Effect size beats p for importance.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Translate a mean difference into real-world terms
questions.stem: A program raises average income by $1,200 with SD $6,000. What is Cohen's d?
questions.explanation: Divide 1,200 by 6,000 to get 0.2, a small effect. The gain is statistically detectable but modest in practical terms.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish correlation from causation in a graph

stimulus.body: A scatterplot shows a strong positive trend between number of fire trucks at a fire and property damage. A headline blames trucks for damage.

questions.stem: What is the most plausible explanation?

options.text: Fire trucks cause additional property damage
Insurance fraud explains all damage
The correlation is actually negative
Larger fires bring more trucks and more damage

questions.explanation: A lurking variable, fire size, drives both. More trucks respond to bigger fires, which also cause more damage, so the causal headline is wrong.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Name a plausible lurking variable
questions.stem: A study finds students who sleep more have higher GPAs. Name a lurking variable and explain its effect.

answer.exemplar: A lurking variable such as academic engagement could increase both sleep regularity and GPA, creating the association without sleep causing grades.

questions.explanation: A third variable can create or inflate an association. Identifying it weakens any causal claim about sleep improving grades.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Identify a limitation of a quasi-experiment
questions.stem: What is the main weakness of a quasi-experimental nonequivalent control group design?

options.text: Groups may differ before treatment
It cannot measure outcomes accurately
It always uses too small a sample
It prevents any data collection

questions.explanation: Without random assignment, pre-existing group differences can masquerade as treatment effects. Measurement quality and sample size are separate issues.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Adjust for baseline differences conceptually
questions.stem: Program group pretest 70, control pretest 64. Program posttest 78, control posttest 70. What is the adjusted gain?
questions.explanation: Program gain is 8 and control gain is 6, so the adjusted gain is 2. Comparing gains removes baseline inequality better than comparing posttests.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS

When participants are adults only
When risk is minimal and consent is impracticable
When the researcher prefers speed

questions.explanation: Waiver requires minimal risk and impracticability of consent, not just anonymity, adulthood, or convenience. Ethics boards make this determination.

questions.stem: Which study most likely qualifies for exempt review?

options.text: Interviews about illegal drug use
Deception about memory performance
Blood draws from children
Benign behavioral observation in public

questions.explanation: Benign public observation is often exempt. Sensitive topics, invasive procedures, and deception usually need more review.

options.text: It shows plausible effects range from small to moderate
It proves the effect is large
It replaces the need for a p-value
It indicates the null is certainly false

questions.explanation: The interval shows the range of plausible effect sizes, from small to moderate, which a p-value alone cannot convey. It complements rather than replaces p.

options.text: Sample standard deviation
Sample size
The sample mean
Confidence level

questions.explanation: The sample mean locates the interval's center but does not change its width. Variability, sample size, and confidence level all affect width.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why effect sizes aid meta-analysis
questions.stem: Why are effect sizes essential for meta-analysis?

answer.exemplar: Meta-analysis combines results across studies; effect sizes put different measures on a common scale, while p-values depend on sample size and cannot be averaged meaningfully.

questions.explanation: Effect sizes standardize findings across studies. P-values are not comparable or combinable in the same way because they scale with sample size.

The drug is clinically essential
The p-value is invalid
The drug has no effect

questions.explanation: A statistically significant 1 mmHg drop is real but clinically trivial. Practical significance requires comparing magnitude to meaningful health thresholds.

Reporting only significant results
Choosing a larger significance level
Using a natural experiment with quasi-random variation

questions.explanation: Natural experiments exploit quasi-random variation to approximate causal identification. More data or relaxed alpha do not fix confounding.

answer.exemplar: Extreme scores tend to move toward the average on retest because of measurement error and natural variability, creating apparent improvement unrelated to treatment.

questions.explanation: Regression to the mean can mimic treatment effects when groups are selected for extreme baseline scores. It is a statistical artifact, not a true gain.

The exact hypothesis being tested
Names of all other participants
Guaranteed personal benefit

A large sample size
A narrow confidence interval
Unmeasured confounding variables

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why small samples yield wide intervals
questions.stem: Why do small samples produce wide confidence intervals?

answer.exemplar: Small samples give imprecise estimates of the standard error, so the margin of error grows and the interval widens to reflect greater uncertainty.

questions.explanation: Less data means more uncertainty in the estimate. The margin of error increases, widening the interval to maintain coverage.

questions.stem: Why can an interrupted time series strengthen causal inference?

options.text: It shows pre-intervention trend and post-intervention change
It uses only one data point

questions.explanation: Interrupted time series compares the pre-existing trend to post-intervention change, helping rule out simple maturation. It does not randomize or replace controls entirely.
